prompt.context: The Sydney Department of Health recently discovered that elderly people (aged above 60) are not satisfied with the medical services they currently receive both in terms of time and quality. Your consulting firm is brought in by the department of health to fix the problem.
prompt.question: What are the main factors you would like to consider in order to improve the medical services for elderly people?

clarifying_info.q: What is the current healthcare process in Sydney?
clarifying_info.a: People typically make an appointment at and visit community medical centres first. If the General Practitioners (doctors in community medical centres) believe patients should be treated in hospitals, the patients will then go to a hospital (also need to make an appointment online).

clarifying_info.q: Which part of the services are elderly people unhappy with?
clarifying_info.a: Elderly people are generally quite happy with the services they received from community medical centres. But they are not happy with the services provided by hospitals.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any other objectives beyond improving medical services?
clarifying_info.a: There are no other objectives other than improving medical services in hospitals for elders.

framework: Customer (Elderly patients) — understand their needs and preferences; how do their needs differ from those under 60?

Processes (where can things go wrong) — break down the patient journey: coming to hospital (booking system, transportation), in hospital (waiting time, treatment quality, hospitalization conditions), out of hospital (follow-up care, insurance reimbursement)
Feasibility (can solutions be implemented?) — funding requirements and government willingness to invest; potential push-backs from hospitals, unions, and other stakeholders

questions.prompt: Q2 (Brainstorm). Our client would like to understand the full customer journey of elderly patients seeking hospital services. Please brainstorm why elderly patients might not be happy at each stage of that journey.
questions.guidance: Candidate should impose a clear structure — the suggested structure is: Coming to Hospital / In Hospital / Out of Hospital. Also acceptable: time-quality-price or other logical frameworks. Great candidates generate at least 5 distinct ideas with logical grouping. Assess on structure and creativity.

questions.prompt: Q3 (Brainstorm). After reviewing the customer journey, it is clear that hospital doctors spend too long diagnosing elderly patients and often make mistakes. What could be the root causes of these issues?
questions.guidance: Suggested structure: People factors vs. Non-people factors. Non-people: hospital medical system may not store elderly patients' medical histories, forcing doctors to spend extra time finding records; medical equipment is old or defective. People (capable but making mistakes): doctors work excessive hours due to staff shortages; lack of incentive or best-practice policies. People (not capable): training or skill gaps. After brainstorming, confirm that the two confirmed root causes are: (1) the medical system does not store medical histories for patients over 60, and (2) hospital doctors are working long hours due to staff shortages.

questions.prompt: Q4 (Calculation). The client wants to convert community medical centre specialists into doctors who exclusively treat elderly patients. There are currently 1,000 such specialists in Sydney. How many additional specialists need to be hired from outside Sydney to treat all elderly patients?
questions.guidance: Push candidate to separately estimate demand (annual elderly visits) and supply (patients one specialist can treat per year) before dividing. Great candidates also discuss whether the resulting number is large or small and whether hiring is feasible.

math.setup: Additional specialists needed = (total elderly visits per year) / (patients per specialist per year) - existing specialists
steps: Sydney population = 16M; ages distribute evenly across 0-80 years, so elderly (>60) share = 20/80 = 25%
Each elderly person visits doctors 4 times per year → annual demand = 4M x 4 = 16M visits
Each specialist treats patients in 30-min slots → 2 patients per hour
Each specialist works 8 hours/day x 5 days/week x 50 weeks/year → 2 x 8 x 5 x 50 = 8,000 patients per year (per casebook)
math.answer: 1,000 additional specialists need to be hired from outside Sydney.

brainstorming.prompt: Brainstorm why elderly patients might not be happy along the full customer journey (coming to hospital, in hospital, out of hospital).

categories.name: Coming to Hospital
ideas: Booking/registration system is not user-friendly for elderly people
Long wait for the earliest available appointment (e.g., 3+ weeks)
Lack of easy public transportation routes to hospitals
Hospitals located too far from elderly patients' homes

categories.name: In Hospital
ideas: Excessive waiting time once inside the hospital
Expensive procedures, specialist fees, or medication costs
Staff with poor or impatient attitudes toward elderly patients

categories.name: Out of Hospital
ideas: Lack of follow-up advice or ongoing care coordination
Difficult or confusing process to reimburse medical insurance bills

recommendation: Elderly patients' dissatisfaction with Sydney hospital services is driven primarily by long treatment times and diagnostic errors, rooted in two confirmed causes: (1) the hospital system does not store medical histories for patients over 60, forcing doctors to spend extra time on each patient; (2) hospital doctors are overworked due to staff shortages.

Establish a dedicated cohort of specialists who exclusively treat elderly patients, converted from community medical centres. This promotes specialization — specialist doctors focus solely on elderly care while hospital doctors can focus on all other patients — and is expected to reduce both treatment time and diagnostic errors.
Hire 1,000 additional specialists from outside Sydney to meet demand. Candidates can be recruited from Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide, or internationally, making the target achievable.
risks: Converting community medical centre specialists may reduce care availability for non-elderly patients at those centres
Recruiting 1,000 specialists requires significant time and cost
Potential push-back from hospital unions or existing staff resistant to role restructuring
next_steps: Upgrade the hospital medical records system to incorporate and make accessible full medical histories for patients over 60
Evaluate quick-win improvements in other parts of the patient journey: registration UX, transportation access, and post-discharge follow-up care
Design incentive and best-practice policies to reduce diagnostic errors independently of staffing changes
